newsitem.title: FRANCE: Russia hopes for Paris deal with NATO on May 27.
newsitem.headline: Russia hopes for Paris deal with NATO on May 27.

text.p: Russia said on Wednesday it hoped to sign a partnership agreement with NATO in Paris on May 27 that would be one of the foundation stones of post-Cold War European security.

Diplomats said the choice of venue strongly suggested the prospect of a "grand deal" in which France and the United States would also settle their dispute over the European role in a reformed Western alliance, enabling Paris to rejoin NATO's integrated military command 30 years after it withdrew.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov announced after talks with French President Jacques Chirac that President Boris Yeltsin had accepted an invitation to come to Paris next month to sign an accord establishing a new, cooperative relationship between NATO and Russia, provided it is ready in time.

"We agreed that if the NATO-Russia agreement can be prepared in the coming weeks and if the preparations are satisfactory to all nations concerned, then the signing by the heads of state or government of the 16 member states and Russia can take place in Paris on May 27," Primakov told an official lunch.
"I am empowered by President Yeltsin to say that the President accepts gratefully the invitation to the signing in Paris if the accord is ready in time," he added.

The minister's two-day trip was part of Moscow's efforts to negotiate conditions for the planned eastward enlargement of NATO that would inflict minimal damage and humiliation on Russia, which opposes the alliance's expansion.

The 16-nation Western defence alliance is expected to invite at least three of Moscow's former Warsaw Pact allies -- Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- to begin NATO membership negotiations at a summit in Madrid in July.

Russia has conceded it cannot stop the expansion, which Primakov once again called "a very grave error", and has sought to win an agreement that NATO will not permanently station troops or build new bases on the territory of new member states.
The United States has said it will not accept any restrictions that give candidate states second-class status.

Diplomatic sources said the negotiations now centred on what constituted "new infrastructure". They believed a formula, sweetened by extra Western economic help, could be found when NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana visits Moscow next Tuesday.

The announcement of a likely Paris summit raised speculation that Chirac was ready to compromise on France's demand for the United States to hand over NATO's southern command, which controls the Mediterranean, to a European officer.
"It enables France to say that it plays a major role in the new NATO," one diplomat close to the negotiations said.
It would be politically difficult for Chirac to host the signing while at the same time delaying France's full return to the alliance, analyst Daniel Vernet wrote in daily Le Monde.

One source said Chirac's diplomatic adviser, Jean-David Levitte, had sketched the outlines of a compromise in talks in Washington on Monday and the United States would discuss the ideas with its senior European allies later this week.
Foreign Minister Herve de Charette would travel to Washington later this month to try to tie up a package deal, French officials said.

They said a compromise might involve splitting the so-called AFSOUTH command into an operational and a territorial command, as existed in the early 1960s when Britain still had a military presence in Malta.

NATO sources say detailed negotiations between the alliance and Russia have advanced since Presidents Bill Clinton and Yeltsin agreed in Helsinki last month to build a partnership meant to ease Moscow's hostility to NATO expansion.

NATO's Brussels headquarters has exchanged draft documents with Moscow and the sources said there was substantial progress on four of the five main points: a preamble on the framework for European security, principles of cooperation, a NATO-Russia joint council and the main areas of cooperation.
